faqs.q: How do Orange homeowners know if their flashing is failing?

runs.v: Water stains on ceilings and walls near a chimney, skylight, or roof-to-wall junction, rusted metal around chimneys, and repeated leaks after patch repairs are the typical signs. Lifted or bent metal at walls and valleys and cracked sealant at a flashing lap also mark damaged flashing, per GAF inspection guidance.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit from Orange for flashing work?

runs.v: Not on a detached one- or two-family house, where repairing or replacing the roof covering counts as ordinary maintenance under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 and needs no construction permit. On a commercial, multi-family, or attached building, repairing more than 25% of the roof area within 12 months requires one. Confirm with the city before work begins.

faqs.q: Does flashing work in an Orange historic district need extra approval?

runs.v: It can. A property inside a locally designated historic district can need design review of exterior work in addition to the construction permit, while National Register listing alone places no restriction on a privately funded repair, per the National Park Service. Confirm a property's status with the city first.

faqs.q: Does caulk fix a flashing leak permanently?

runs.v: No. Caulk alone is a temporary flashing repair, because sealant dries and cracks within a few years while properly lapped, corrosion-resistant metal sheds water without relying on it, per GAF technical guidance.

faqs.q: How much does roof flashing installation repair cost in Orange, NJ?

runs.v: A flashing reseal or small section costs $200–$500 per Modernize cost data, and a chimney flashing repair runs $300–$1,800, with most repairs $400–$1,600, per HomeGuide and Angi. A larger chimney or valley rebuild that lifts and reinstalls the surrounding shingles costs more.

faqs.q: How do I fix the flashing on my roof?

runs.v: Find the failed detail first, then repair it in metal: refasten and reseal a loose counter-flashing edge, replace a cracked pipe boot, and replace corroded step flashing piece by piece, lifting the shingles and siding so each new piece overlaps the one below it. Replacing flashing on a steep or multi-story roof is safest left to a registered, insured roofer.
